close_reason: Landed in ed75b38 (paired with .17). Threat-model section explicitly scopes safe (public-blob integrity, the in-scope CID draft use case) vs unsafe (MAC verification, commitment opening, capability-token comparison) uses. Explains why no ct_eq helper ships from this crate (workspace policy: MAC/HMAC verification belongs on a separate type so constant-time equality is part of the type contract).
description:
Crypto-security supplement complementary to JMAP-sf5h.17 (which flags that the variable-time `PartialEq` is undocumented). This finding scopes the workspace decision rather than just the docs gap.

draft-atwood-jmap-cid-00 uses SHA-256 of public blobs for integrity verification — the digest is server-published and broadcast to anyone with read access to the blob. In that threat model, variable-time `PartialEq` is **fine**: there is no secret value being compared against the digest, so the timing channel reveals nothing an attacker doesn't already have.

However, consumers may repurpose `Sha256` for use cases where the timing channel **does** matter:

1. **MAC-style verification** — comparing an expected digest (delivered out-of-band, possibly as a secret commitment) against a computed digest. Per-byte short-circuit compare reveals how many leading bytes match, enabling secret recovery in the classic Bleichenbacher-class pattern.
2. **Commitment opening** — comparing a presented preimage's digest against a committed digest where the commitment is secret-derived.
3. **Capability tokens** — using a digest as an unforgeable bearer credential.

The `Sha256` type derives `PartialEq` (digest.rs:99), which does byte-by-byte short-circuit compare via `String`'s `PartialEq`. This is exploitable for use cases (1)-(3) but irrelevant for the in-scope JMAP CID use case.

**Fix** — choose one:

(a) **Document narrow scope**. Add a rustdoc `# Threat model` section to `Sha256` stating: "This type carries a SHA-256 digest of a public blob. `PartialEq` is variable-time and is appropriate for integrity verification of public data. Consumers performing MAC verification, commitment opening, or any comparison where the expected digest is secret-derived MUST use a constant-time compare via `subtle::ConstantTimeEq` on the underlying bytes — extract via `.as_str().as_bytes()` or via a `to_bytes(&self) -> [u8; 32]` helper if added." This is the minimum-cost option; aligns with JMAP-sf5h.17 framing.

(b) **Provide a `ct_eq` method gated on `subtle`**. Add an optional `subtle` dep and a `ct_eq(&self, other: &Self) -> subtle::Choice` method that compares the underlying 32 raw bytes (not the hex string — comparing hex would compare 64 bytes and is still constant-time but doubles the work). Requires a `to_bytes()` accessor that parses the hex back to `[u8; 32]`, which depends on JMAP-sf5h.18 (the inner-representation question) being settled.

(c) **Defend the do-nothing posture**. Cite that the JMAP CID draft has no MAC-style usage, no consumer in this workspace will ever use `Sha256` for secret comparison, and any future need would warrant a separate type (`MacTag`, `SecretDigest`).

Recommend (a) for now — minimal cost, scopes the existing JMAP-sf5h.17 docs gap to a specific threat model. Re-evaluate (b) when the .18 inner-representation question is decided and the byte-level API exists naturally.

What goes wrong if left as-is: a downstream library that imports `jmap-cid-types` to express "a SHA-256 wire value" — entirely reasonable given the crate's general name — and uses it for MAC verification, will leak its expected digest one byte at a time to a remote attacker. The crate's docs currently give no signal that this is a misuse.

title: Sha256 threat-model documentation gap: variable-time PartialEq is OK for public-blob integrity but unsuitable for MAC verification
